newsitem.title: USA: Lawmaker asks will IRS study student report cards?.
newsitem.headline: Lawmaker asks will IRS study student report cards?.

text.p: A congressman asked Thursday if the Internal Revenue Service would examine student report cards and if teachers could be pressured into giving better grades under President Clinton's scholarship tax plan.

Questioning details of Clinton's Hope Scholarship proposal, House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Bill Archer has asked the Treasury Department how the government would monitor a college student's grades for a proposed tax credit.

"I understand the president's budget will include the 'Hope Scholarship' initiative announced during the campaign that features a tax deduction and a tax credit contingent on a student's receiving a 'B' average," Archer said in a letter to Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin.

"How will the federal government know if a student has a 'B' average? Will the Internal Revenue Service collect students' report cards in the same manner in which they obtain written reports to verify other tax data?" Archer asked.

Other questions he asked included whether the proposal would drive up the cost of college and whether it would put teachers under pressure to give students B averages. The letter from the Texas Republican, dated Wednesday, was released Thursday.

"The secretary will respond to Chairman Archer's letter," a Treasury spokesman said. "This proposal, and all of the proposals in the budget that will be submitted on Feb. 6, have been refined and worked on through an interagency process."
Far from being dismayed by Archer's letter, the White House said it viewed Archer's questions as evidence that Republicans were taking the president's proposals seriously.

"It asked very serious and legitimate questions," White House spokesman Mike McCurry said at his daily briefing. "So far, based on the comments coming from some of the Republican leaders on the Hill, they're taking what we're saying seriously and the president is very encouraged by that."
"Hopefully, we are creating an environment here in which we can make progress sooner, rather than later, on a balanced budget agreement," he added.

Archer also asked how the differences in the tax year, a calendar year, and the school year, divided into semesters, would be resolved. Would a student with a C+ average in the fall and a B+ average in the spring of the following year qualify for the credit?

"The principle of using the tax code to help provide for affordable educational opportunities represents common ground, but I await your reply in order to evaluate the merits of this particular tax proposal," Archer wrote.
On another contentious tax issue, President Clinton appeared to hold out an olive branch to Republicans, saying on television he was willing to be flexible on a capital gains tax cut.
Republicans have sought a broad-based capital gains tax cut, while Democrats have proposing a targeted approach of capital gains tax reduction in specific areas.
